In Ti alloys the β-phase usually favors superplasticity by promoting grain boundary sliding along the interphase boundaries [13]. In the Ti–6A1–4V alloy the appearance of even a small amount of β-phase during the heating most likely also makes contribution to superplasticity by inhibiting significant grain growth and promotion of grain boundary sliding.

Such unusual superplastic behavior of the alloy at the reduced strain rate sensitivity can most likely be explained by taking into account significant hardening of the alloy during the deformation. According to Hart's suggestion [18] the stability of flow can be achieved by increasing the strain rate sensitivity of the flow stress as well as from strain hardening.

TEM investigations showed the formation of UFG microstructure in this alloy during HPT and subsequent heat treatment. This process is accompanied by precipitation of β-phase. Such microstructure promotes stability of ultra-fine grains during superplastic deformation.

Perhaps the enhanced grain boundary diffusion that has been observed in such UFG microstructure [3] acts to relax the local stress concentration that is needed to nucleate cavities at the grain boundaries.

An important aspect of microstructural evolution in the Ti–6A1–4V alloy, processed by severe plastic deformation, is the very high strength obtained after superplastic deformation, which is outstanding for this alloy.
In contrast to previous specimen, this one showed the complete grain structure.

It is possible that this increase in room temperature strength after superplastic deformation in this UFG Ti alloy is associated with lack of cavitation as well as with the smallness of the retained grain size.
